content: Resistant starch (RS) is a type of starch that is not digested in the small intestine of healthy individuals. Instead, it passes into the large intestine, where it functions similarly to dietary fiber. Resistant starch is classified as the third type of dietary fiber because it provides benefits associated with both insoluble and soluble fibers. Most carbohydrates, such as sugars and common starches, are rapidly digested and absorbed in the small intestine as glucose, which is then used for immediate energy or stored for later use. Resistant starch, however, resists digestion and reaches the large intestine intact, where it acts like dietary fiber. Resistant starch is categorized into four types: 1. RS1: This type is physically inaccessible or indigestible starch, found in foods like seeds, legumes, and unprocessed whole grains. 2. RS2: This type occurs naturally in its granular form, such as in uncooked potatoes, green banana flour, and high-amylose corn. 3. RS3: This type forms when starchy foods are cooked and then cooled, such as in bread, cornflakes, and cooked-and-chilled potatoes. It is also found in retrograded high-amylose corn. 4. RS4: These are chemically modified starches designed to resist digestion. They have diverse structures and are not naturally occurring. Resistant starch is one of three types of dietary fiber. Soluble fibers, such as pectins, gums, and mucilages, are found in fruits, vegetables, oats, legumes, and seeds. Some soluble fibers increase the viscosity of intestinal contents, aiding in cholesterol reduction, while others are fermented by gut bacteria, promoting colon health and enhancing mineral absorption. Insoluble fibers, such as cellulose and lignin, are found in plant cell walls, whole grain products, fruits, and vegetables. These fibers are not fermented and primarily aid in maintaining regular bowel movements. Natural resistant starch is insoluble, fermented in the large intestine, and acts as a prebiotic fiber. Other types of resistant starch may be either soluble or insoluble and may or may not have prebiotic properties. Foods naturally rich in resistant starch include legumes, bananas (especially under-ripe, green bananas), and unprocessed whole grains. Public health experts recognize a significant gap between the amount of fiber most people consume and the optimal amount needed for health. The National Academy of Sciences recommends a daily intake of 38 grams for adult men and 25 grams for adult women. Many countries suggest a daily fiber intake of 25–30 grams. Resistant starch can help increase dietary fiber intake without altering the taste or texture of foods, making it a practical addition to various food products. The National Academy of Sciences acknowledges resistant starch as a beneficial carbohydrate. Research on natural resistant starches, particularly from high-amylose corn, has demonstrated benefits for intestinal and colonic health, as well as metabolic advantages such as improved glycemic management and energy regulation. Different classes of resistant starch are digested and fermented differently, necessitating individual consideration. Weight Management Consuming foods containing natural resistant starch supports weight management in three ways: 1. Fiber Fortification: Adding resistant starch to foods like bread, biscuits, pasta, and cereals increases fiber content without affecting taste or texture. The World Health Organization has identified dietary fiber as the only dietary component with convincing evidence of a protective effect against weight gain and obesity. Fiber increases satiety, reduces hunger, and may influence hormone secretion related to digestion. 2. Calorie Reduction: Resistant starch lowers the caloric content of foods when it replaces flour or other rapidly digested carbohydrates. Natural resistant starch provides 2–3 kilocalories per gram, compared to 4 kilocalories per gram for typical carbohydrates. 3. Lipid Oxidation: Resistant starch promotes fat burning and may reduce fat accumulation. Clinical trials with high-amylose corn resistant starch have shown increased fat oxidation after meals and altered the body's energy utilization, prioritizing fat burning over carbohydrates and protein. Energy Management Eating foods with natural resistant starch helps balance energy levels after meals by mitigating blood sugar drops. Resistant starch releases part of its energy as glucose in the small intestine, which is essential for brain function, and part as fermentation by-products in the large intestine, which serve as energy sources for muscle and fat tissue. This slow energy release results in moderate blood sugar rises and helps regulate the rapid spikes caused by processed carbohydrates. Such glycemic stability is particularly beneficial as people age, when energy fluctuations become more common. Blood Sugar Response and Glycemic Management Natural resistant starch helps maintain healthy blood sugar levels by increasing insulin sensitivity in healthy individuals. When used as a flour substitute, it reduces the glycemic impact of foods and enhances insulin sensitivity, potentially lowering the risk of type 2 diabetes. High-glycemic diets can lead to insulin resistance, where cells become less responsive to insulin, increasing the risk of diabetes. Resistant starch consumption has been shown to decrease glycemic responses in both healthy individuals and diabetics, while also improving insulin sensitivity. Digestive and Colonic Health Natural resistant starch supports colon and digestive health through several mechanisms. It promotes regular bowel movements with a mild laxative effect. Fermentation of resistant starch in the large intestine lowers intestinal pH and reduces the production of harmful compounds like secondary bile acids, ammonia, and phenols. It also produces short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), such as butyrate, which is the primary energy source for colonic cells and has anti-inflammatory properties. Butyrate is particularly important for colon health, as it supports healthy colon cells and has anti-carcinogenic effects. Research has shown that butyrate inhibits tumor cell growth, induces differentiation of tumor cells into normal-like cells, and triggers apoptosis (programmed cell death) in colorectal cancer cells. Resistant starch also contributes to oral rehydration solutions for treating diarrhea. Gluten-Free Applications Resistant starch can replace wheat products in gluten-free foods. Recent studies suggest that resistant starch fermentation in the colon produces more butyrate than other tested fibers. Butyrate's anti-carcinogenic and anti-inflammatory properties may be beneficial for preventing or treating conditions like celiac disease and inflammatory bowel disease.
